s08.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:45 PM · THE ATCHAFALAYA BASIN BRIDGE — WASH YOUR FACE
body: Past Baton Rouge the land goes wet and then gives up, and the interstate climbs onto its concrete legs and stays there, two spans side by side running out over the Basin for eighteen miles, with the sun dead ahead of them now and going. There’s no heron this time. The water under the cypress is empty and black, and the light drains out of it from the bottom up while the treetops keep a little copper.

Kevin drives with the visor down and his eyes narrowed to slits. Theo has the other middle chair, his loafers off and his socked feet up on the console between them. In the way-back Laney is typing with both thumbs, a steady plastic clicking, and Lena is somewhere behind Jack’s headrest, where he can’t see her without turning around, and he doesn’t turn around.
The RAZR goes off in his breast pocket, alone in there, against the place the tin wore into the lining. SKYE (MISFIT).
“Hey,” he says.
“Hi.”
Just her, first thing, with nobody in front of her; he doesn’t know what to make of that, and then she’s going.

“I’m in my trailer in a robe with my hair in forty pins. I have twelve minutes, and there’s a wig on a foam head on the counter watching me like it’s heard things. Tonight a truck rains on me again. Show me your dirt.”
“My what?”
“Your *dirt*, Jack. Your ashes. It’s been Wednesday all day where you are, and I want to see it before you sweat it off or Ted licks his thumb and fixes it. Picture. Now. I’ll hold.”

He turns the RAZR around in his hand so the little lens on the hinge looks back at him and holds it out at the end of his arm, aiming at nothing he can see. The first one is the van’s headliner and half an eyebrow. The second is his nose and a piece of Louisiana. Across the aisle Theo leans over with a helpful hand out. “The subject doesn’t —”
“I’ve got it.”

The third one has it: one eye squinted against the sun, and over it Father Hébert’s thumb, a gray cross leaning left like a fence post after a Youngstown winter. *New Picture Msg.* He sends it and puts the phone back to his ear and waits.
What comes out of the RAZR is a shriek, delighted and enormous, loud enough that the van hears it and Kevin’s eyes come up to the mirror.
“Is she okay?” Kevin says.
“She got the picture.”

“Oh, *look* at you. Hold still. Madame Skye will read it.” And there she is after all, a boardwalk booth with a beaded curtain, bangles going on both wrists. “Madame Skye sees… a long journey. Many miles. A van. A coconut — why is there a coconut —”
“Long story.”
“Madame Skye charges by the minute. She sees a man in a dress —”
“Vestments.”

“A man in a *robe*, forgive me, Father. An old man. His thumb, it shakes.” The bangles slow. “But he pressed hard. Look at that. He leaned in.” Madame goes back behind her curtain, and it’s Skye, in a trailer in Burnaby, looking at a stamp-sized picture of his face. “That’s a good thumb, Jack. That man meant it.”
“He’s seventy-four.”
“He meant it at seventy-four. That’s harder. What did he say when he did it?”
“Remember that you are dust, and to dust you will return.” He looks at the cypress going by. “Then he said something in French.”
“What did he say in French?”
“*Le garçon de l’Ohio.* The boy from Ohio.”
“He *knows* you.”
“He’s met me twice.”

“Twice is plenty, for a man who leans in.” Paper rustles on her end; she has printed something out again. “Okay. Real question. I read it, the one they read today, Matthew six. I found it on a church website with a dove that flaps its wings when you scroll. It’s the only scripture with a makeup note. *Wash your face, so nobody can tell you’re fasting.* And then you all walk around all day with dirt on it. Explain it.”
He knows exactly how small the van is, how well a voice carries in it from the middle chairs to the back. He answers her anyway, because she asked it straight.

“The fast is the part nobody sees,” he says. “That’s Matthew six. That’s between you and Him, so you keep your face clean and it stays that way. The ashes aren’t that. The ashes don’t say *look how holy I am*. They say *I’m going to die*. Remember you’re dust. And everybody gets the same thumb — the bishop, the lady from the dry cleaner’s, the guy with the bad hip in the back pew. You don’t pick it out, and you can’t do it well.” He looks for the rest and finds it in his father’s mouth. “My dad says when Campbell Works was still running, every man on the shift came out the gate the same gray. Nobody at the bar after thought the soot made you a good steelworker. It just meant you’d been in there with everybody else. And you wash it off at night. It’s not supposed to make it to tomorrow.”
Behind him, in the way-back, the clicking has stopped.
Skye is quiet. Then: “So it’s a costume that isn’t allowed to be a performance.”
“Yes.”
“That’s the hardest note there is.” She says it like a professional, and he believes her; it’s her job.
“Kyle’s doing Lent, by the way. He’s giving up the Colts. He came into the makeup trailer this morning and said it to the mirror like a wedding vow. Russ cried. I think Russ cried.”
“Is Kyle Catholic?”
“Kyle is from Indianapolis. It’s close.” A pin goes into something on her end. “I’m doing it too,” she says. “Lent.”
“What are you giving up?”
“Matthew six, Jack. I read the fine print.”
He waits, and she lets him wait, and he can hear her enjoying it.

body.text: “Also. You told me to go be brilliant. I was brilliant. Ask the goose. The goose was there for all six hours. The goose wept.”
body.else: “Also. The goose saw your bag picture. The goose thinks it’s a cry for help.”

body.text: “And I’ve started the binder. It has tabs.”
“What’s on the tabs?”
“Fridays. Cigarettes. Loopholes. Loopholes is the thickest tab.”
“Did you say one for me this morning?”
“I offered the whole thing.”
“The *what*?”
“Lent. All of it.”
On her end, nothing at all. Then: “Well. Okay. That’s a lot of Lent.”
“Did you say one for me this morning?”
“I did.”
“A good one?”
“On my knees on a kneeler older than my dad.”
“Good. I said I’d hold you to it.”
“So. For real this time?”
“For real.”
“Good. I’m holding you to it. I have a very strong grip. Ask anybody I’ve ever shaken hands with at a premiere.”

body: She brings the phone in close; he can tell by the way the trailer goes away behind her. “Wash it off tonight,” she says, low, right against his ear. “Like the book says. And Tuesday you come up the hill clean, and I’m going to find out if any of it comes off on my pillowcase.”
Tuesday. She has it written down somewhere in that trailer, in a hand he’d know anywhere. He looks out at the black water going by under the bridge.
“I’m in a van, Skye.”
“I know. I can hear Ted breathing through his mouth.”
Across the aisle Theo shuts his mouth.
He loves her. It’s as much a fact as the bridge, concrete under all six of them, and every word he has said to her on it is true.
Behind him, low, Laney says something to the way-back, and gets no answer.
On her end someone knocks and says a number through a door. “That’s me,” Skye says, and then, fast: “Six days. I’m counting. I don’t count.” A little sound, the robe or the pins. “Bye, Dust.”

choices.key: On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. “Six days,” you said.
response: “Six days,” he says.
“Six,” she says, and is gone. He keeps the shut phone in his fist until the bridge comes down onto dry land.

choices.text: “Whatever you’re giving up — it’s a good present.”
choices.key: On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. You told her whatever she was giving up, it was a good present.
response: “Whatever you’re giving up,” he says, “it’s a good present.”
On her end there’s a silence that isn’t a bit, long enough for the knock to come again. “Okay,” she says — just that — and hangs up first. The RAZR sits shut on his knee, warm from his ear.

choices.key: On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. You gave her back her old goodbye, and she laughed.
response: “Bye, Coat check.”
She laughs, startled and delighted, all the way into the dial tone.

s08a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:15 PM · HOUSTON, A GAS STATION OFF I-10
body: Through Lafayette nobody says much. In the rearview, past Kevin’s ear, Lena has her face turned to the window and the dark going by in it, and Laney’s hand is on her knee, and at Lake Charles the hand is still there.

On the west side of Houston, Kevin brings them in under a canopy lit so white it takes the color out of everybody: twelve pumps, a store that’s a wall of glass, a man in a Texans cap filling a bass boat. Jack takes the nozzle. Through the glass, on a television bracketed over the cigarette rack, the snowboarder goes up a wall of snow on the replay with his red hair out behind him, turns over in the air, lands, and goes up again, the sound off.
Lena comes around the back of the van with her LG in her hand, lit. On its outside screen, small and white: JULIAN.
She looks at it. She walks past the pumps to the ice machine at the end of the store, turns her back to the island, and answers it.

Four minutes by the clock over the door. He can see all of it and hear none of it: her free hand pushed down into the jean jacket’s pocket, her head down, the ice machine’s blue sign on her hair. Once she nods. Once she puts her hand on the ice machine’s lid and leaves it there. The pump clicks off. He hangs up the nozzle and screws the cap on and waits for the receipt, and the receipt takes its time.
She shuts the phone and comes back across the concrete and climbs into the way-back past Laney’s knees, and says nothing, and nobody asks her anything.
Margot holds out her hand for the keys. On Kevin’s sheet, in the glovebox under the registration, the next line says MARGOT — SAN ANTONIO.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 2:40 AM · I-10 WEST, PAST SONORA — THE NAVIGATOR
body: Kevin’s sheet gives Jack San Antonio to Fort Stockton and gives the seat beside him to Theo. West of Junction the Hill Country lets go of its hills one at a time, and out here past Sonora there’s nothing left for the headlights to find but the white line and the bar ditch, and now and then two green coins low in the ditch that don’t blink and don’t move — a deer — and then they’re behind him. The cruise is set at seventy-two. The dash clock is the only light in the van that isn’t the road’s.

Theo has the atlas on his knees, open to Texas, a church bulletin keeping Arizona. Jack looks at it there. The last time it was three in the morning in Texas, that atlas rode on somebody else’s knees, going the other way.

Everybody else is asleep. Kevin is folded across a middle chair with his windbreaker over his face. Margot sleeps upright against her window with her mouth shut, declining to comment even unconscious. In the way-back Laney is a heap of pashmina with the coconut’s crown sticking out of it, and beside her Lena lies on her side with her knees drawn up. A truck goes by the other way, and its lights come through the van and lift her face out of the dark in the rearview — gray, eyes shut — and put it back. That’s all the mirror tells him.
He has had the sentence since Lake Charles. He has turned it over so many times crossing Texas that the corners have worn off it, and it still isn’t any lighter.
Theo is awake. Theo is usually awake at this hour; in 412 it’s the laptop light on his face at two and three, and here it’s the dash, green.
“Is the coconut legal in California,” Theo says, eventually.
“It’s dead. It’s painted.”

“It’s a fruit, Costigan. There’s an inspection station at Blythe. Laney’s been rehearsing since breakfast.” Theo puts his head back against the rest. “Picture it. A checkpoint at dusk. A woman in sunglasses. A coconut in sequins, with everything to lose.”
“It’s not a checkpoint.”
“Tell Coco.”
“How’s Hale?”
“One sentence.”
“Four thousand words due Monday, and you have one sentence.”
“It’s a good sentence.”
“He’ll have it framed,” Theo says. “Then he’ll fail you under the frame.”

A while later he says they gave the snowboarder the gold, and Jack says he saw it through a window in Houston, and Theo says he doesn’t understand how they score it, and Jack doesn’t either, and that’s the Olympics.
“I’ve been trying to figure out what I gave up,” Theo says, with the atlas open on Arizona. “Kevin won’t tell me.”
Jack has nothing for that, so he drives.

West of the next exit a doe comes up out of the bar ditch and stands in the right lane, gray in the high beams, her ears turned toward them. Jack is off the cruise and standing on the brake, and the van noses down and everything loose in it slides forward, and the doe takes two long unhurried steps and is over the median and gone. Theo has one hand braced on the dash. Behind them Kevin says something into his windbreaker and doesn’t wake. Jack eases back up through sixty and seventy and sets the cruise again, and his heart goes on banging a long time after, like somebody at a door.

Then nothing for a long time: the tires, the heater, the white line coming at them out of the dark and going under. The radio is on scan, and on scan out here it mostly finds static and a man selling feed, until a station somewhere in West Texas comes up clear with Emmylou Harris on it, and the scan stops there. Theo reaches over and turns it down. Not off.

“‘Boulder to Birmingham,’” he says. “She wrote it after Gram Parsons died. He died out in the desert, at Joshua Tree, and his friends stole the body out of the airport and drove it back out there and burned it. Because he’d asked them to.”
“That’s a true story?”
“Hand to God.” Theo looks at the radio. “Some people get a friend like that.”
They listen to a verse of it. Jack checks the mirror. The way-back is dark, and nothing moves in it, and he looks at the road again.
“Theo.”
“Costigan.”
“I’m ending it with Skye. Tuesday. When she’s back.”
It’s the first time he’s said it out loud to anybody. It sounds smaller in the van than it did in his head, and truer, and it can’t be put back.
Theo turns his head and looks out his window. There’s nothing out there. He looks at it anyway, for as long as the song takes to get to its chorus and past it.
“Okay,” he says.
And after a while: “Okay.”
Jack waits. The next question is right there in the van with them, close enough to pick up off the dash, and Theo turns around in his seat and looks straight at it and doesn’t ask it.
“Don’t tell me anything else.”
“I wasn’t going to.”
“Good.” Theo faces front. “Don’t.”

His iPhone is on his thigh. He wakes it, and his thumb opens something, and hangs over the glass, and types nothing. He locks it and turns it face down on his leg. Jack doesn’t have to guess who he isn’t writing to.

Jack watches the white line. He knows exactly why Theo won’t hear the rest — two nights ago on the levee it got a name — and he gives nothing away. Neither does Theo, except that he has shut the atlas on his own finger and left it there.
A few miles on, a blue sign comes up with a picnic table on it.
“Pull off.”
“You okay?”
“Pull off, Costigan.”

It’s three concrete tables under three tin roofs and a windbreak of cedars all leaning the same way, and nobody. Jack pulls in and stops with the headlights on the cedars. Theo gets out, and the cold comes in where he was, and he walks out past the tables, past the end of the light, and stops. Jack can just make him out: his back to the van, both hands on top of his head with the fingers laced, the way guys stood at the foul line at the rec center after the last game of a bad season.

He stands like that a minute. The engine ticks. When Jack leans to look up through the windshield, the sky over the cedars is crowded down to the ground. Jack keeps his hands on the wheel. He could get out. He doesn’t; Theo walked a long way into the dark to stand with his back to the van. In the way-back nobody stirs. Emmylou goes on low to the cedars, and gets to the end, and the station goes back to a man reading the weather for Pecos County.
Theo comes back across the light with his hands in his blazer pockets and gets in and shuts the door and puts his belt on.
“Leg cramp,” he says.

Jack puts it in drive. Out on the interstate a westbound rig goes by with every running light it owns lit up, amber and red all down its length, a carnival with somewhere to be, and is gone up the road.
They’re back up to seventy-two when Theo says, “She’s —”
“I know.”
“Callender’s going to —”
“I know, Theo.”
“She sent me a picture of your violets,” Theo says. “On Sunday. In the trailer. No caption.” He stops there.

Theo rubs his eyes with the heels of both hands. He has known her since they were kids under the craft-services table on the Meridian lots, rating everybody’s outfits; he has been her Ted longer than Jack has been anybody’s anything.
“Be good to her,” Theo says. “Tuesday. Just — be good to her.”

choices.text: “I will. She gets the truth, the whole thing, to her face. It’s the best thing I’ve got.”
choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him. You promised him she’d get the whole truth, to her face.
response: “I will,” Jack says. “She gets the truth. The whole thing, to her face. It’s the best thing I’ve got.”
Theo nods at the windshield. “It is,” he says. “It’s the best thing you’ve got.” The song ends under it, and the West Texas station goes to static, and neither of them reaches for the knob.

choices.text: “I love her, Theo. That’s the part that doesn’t help.”
choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him — and that you love her, and it doesn’t help.
response: “I love her, Theo,” he says. “That’s the part that doesn’t help.”
“No,” Theo says. “It never does.” He opens the atlas again and finds where they are in the dash light with one finger, a blue line in a lot of white, and looks at it, and closes it.

choices.text: “You introduced us. I’m putting it on your tab.”
choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him. You put it on his tab.
response: “You introduced us,” Jack says. “I’m putting it on your tab.”

“I owe you a kidney,” Theo says. It’s meant for a joke and doesn’t land as one, and neither of them tries another. Around five the lights of Fort Stockton come up out of the flat ahead, a handful of orange on the black, and Theo points at them without a word.

choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him. Then you drove.
response: Jack nods, and drives. Seventy-two on the cruise. The white line coming and going under. Beside him Theo reaches over and turns the radio back up one notch, and that’s the end of talking till Fort Stockton.

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 7:40 AM · FORT STOCKTON, A TRUCK STOP OFF I-10 — THE FOURTEENTH MORNING
body: They pulled in at five, per the sheet, and everybody slept two hours across the seats but Jack and Theo.

Now the sun is up over the flat behind them, low and white, and every rig in the lot throws a shadow a hundred feet long toward New Mexico. It’s the dry cold of the high desert in February, the kind that goes through denim like it isn’t there. Kevin stands at the driver’s door doing hamstring stretches with the keys already in his fist. Lena is at the back bumper with a coffee in both hands and her hood up, out of the wind, at the edge of everything. Through the truck stop’s window a television over the coffee island shows a skier coming down a mountain on the replay, gold, the sound off.
In the men’s room Jack washes his face at a steel sink, and the last of Wednesday comes off his hairline gray and goes down the drain.

Margot sits sideways in the passenger seat with the door open and her boots on the running board and a paperback on her knee. When he comes back across the lot she holds out the Gideon without looking up from her page: small, green, worn to the weave at the corners, SANTA LUCIA MOTOR COURT stamped purple inside the board. The fourteenth morning.

He doesn’t need it. He leans on the van’s cold flank and says it into the cold from memory — *He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two* — the staff and the sandals, *no food, no sack, no money in their belts*, with Gloria’s ones folded in the wallet against his hip, and the dust at the end, shaken off your feet. He hands the book back. Margot takes it with her eyes still on the paperback and puts it in her coat.

His hands won’t stay anywhere. He has a bottle of water from inside, and he takes the label off it in strips with his thumbnail, one, then the next, till it’s bare, and starts on the glue. He cracks his knuckles, all of them, twice. He drums on the roof rack until Laney, inside, says “Jack. *Please*,” and then he drums on his own leg. Under the skin on the insides of his forearms something crawls that scratching can’t get to, and he scratches anyway. The coffee is his second and hasn’t touched the fog. And under all of it is the want — not a cigarette so much as the business of one, the cellophane coming off in one pull, the flick, the first drag going down to the bottom of him — so exact he can taste the filter. Every fight he’s had since August ended there. He has a fight in him right now and nowhere to put it.

Kevin watches him over the top of the driver’s door. “It’s not the nicotine,” he says. “You smoke like it’s a holy day of obligation. It’s the hands — the habit’s been told no.” He swings up into the seat. “Textbook. Tired and hungry makes it worse. Respectfully, you’re a hazard to navigation.”
“He’s not a patient, Kevin,” Laney says from inside.
“Everybody’s a patient, Laney.” Kevin adjusts his mirror. “Some of us are just in the waiting room.”

To give his hands a job, Jack gets out Hale’s legal pad and sits on the step of the open side door with it on his knee: THE SECOND LINE across the top, the one good sentence under it, and the bottom of the pad ragged where six strips came off in an attic in Mid-City. He clicks the pen. His hand wants to be doing something else, and he makes it do this instead, and starts the second paragraph.

body.text: *Then a trumpet player found me in the crowd and pointed the bell at me, as though the song had been looking for the man worst at it, to make him go first.*
body.else: *From the curb you can watch the second line go by and believe it has nothing to do with you, which is what curbs are for.*

body: Theo comes around the front of the van with Coco under his arm like a football and a coffee in his other hand. “Fun fact,” he says. “She’s not technically a nut. She’s a drupe. Laney should lead with that at Blythe. It’s a completely different —”
“Nobody cares, Theo.” Jack doesn’t look up from the pad. “Nobody in this van has cared about one thing out of your mouth since August that wasn’t about you.”

He hears it land. Theo stands there with the coconut and the coffee. Then he sets the coffee on the van’s roof, very carefully, and presses the lid down around its rim, though there was nothing wrong with the lid.
By the back bumper, Lena, with her own coffee in both hands, looks at the ground.

response: “Sorry, Theo,” he says. “That wasn’t you.”

“It was a little me.” Theo takes his coffee down off the roof and hands Jack the coconut to hold while he climbs in. It’s generous, and quick, and Jack sits there on the step holding a painted coconut, forgiven before he’s finished being ashamed.

choices.text: “I’d like to apologize to the coconut.”
response: “I’d like to apologize to the coconut,” he says.
From inside the van, Laney: “*She* accepts.” Theo takes his coffee down off the roof and climbs in past him with Coco. He doesn’t say whether he does.

He bends over the pad. Theo stands there a second longer; then he takes his coffee down off the roof and gets in with the coconut and lets it go, and Jack would rather have been hit. He writes half a page he’ll cross out in El Paso.

s11.slug: THURSDAY · 10:20 AM · EL PASO, A GAS STATION OFF I-10 — THE AIR PUMP
body: “We gained an hour,” Kevin says, past Van Horn, when the dash clock and the RAZR stop agreeing. He reaches over and sets the clock back with the tip of a pen. “I’m logging it.”
By El Paso Jack has two pages.

It’s the same station. He knows it from the off-ramp: six islands under the canopy, chain-link past the last of them, and below the grade of the interstate the concrete channel with the line down the middle and Juárez on the other side, poured up the side of its mountain, which at midnight was a lamp left on and at ten in the morning is just a city, tan and pink and enormous, with laundry on its roofs. The square of cardboard is still taped over the card reader on pump four. PAY INSIDE AFTER 10 PM. Kevin reads it aloud anyway.

At the edge of the lot, where the concrete gives out into gravel, is the air pump. Jack doesn’t look at it. He knows where it is without looking. The seventeenth rides in a tin in her jacket now, dated in his hand; she was asleep in the van forty feet from it when he lit it, and didn’t know till the levee.

Inside, the store’s radio is on an El Paso station, or a Juárez one, and Selena is singing “Como la Flor” over the hot-dog rollers, and the woman at the register sings the end of every line along with her, a hair behind. Jack pours a coffee. He puts the lid on. He sets it on the counter, and he hears himself ask for a pack of Marlboro Reds before he knows he’s going to, the way you’d hear somebody behind you in line.

Behind her the cigarettes stand in their slots up the wall, every brand in its row like bolts in a hardware bin. She takes a red box down from its slot by feel and puts it on the counter. “¿Algo más?” — “No. Gracias.” His Spanish is the Anchor’s dish pit, Rudy’s, about forty words and most of them about pans. Five and change. He pays out of the fold of Gloria’s ones in his wallet, his fingers not quite steady on them, counting them out face up and all facing one direction: Gloria’s rule for tips.

He walks out with the coffee in one hand and the pack in the other. At pump four Kevin has the hood up and is reading the dipstick in the sun, and Margot is doing the windshield with the squeegee in long exact strokes, and Laney is asleep against the back glass with her mouth open. He walks past all of it, across the lot, and stands under the air pump.

Nobody’s using it. AIR 75¢, and the hose hanging in a loop off its hook, and under it a dark ring on the concrete where cars have dripped for years. Twelve days ago he stood on that ring at five to midnight and lit the last one.

Through the store’s open door Selena is still going. Rudy keeps a radio over the fryer at the Anchor tuned to a station out of Oxnard, and on Saturday nights Jack has scraped a few thousand plates to this song without ever knowing what it was called, and here it is, in El Paso, where it belongs.

He sets the coffee on top of the pump. The pack is lighter than he remembers and heavier than it should be. The cellophane is tight and cold and takes the sun. The red tear strip runs around under the lid with its little tab standing up, waiting for a thumbnail. He can smell it through the plastic, or thinks he can — the sweet brown smell that lived in his father’s truck and in the Carhartt and at the end of every argument he ever walked out of. His thumbnail finds the tab and rests there.

His hands are still. All morning they’ve been at the label on a water bottle and the roof rack and his own knuckles, and now, with this in them, they’re quiet as a sleeping dog, and that’s the worst thing he’s found out about himself in Texas.
He doesn’t open it.

If it’s in his pocket, he chooses every hour, all the way to Easter. If it’s in the trash can by the door, he’s at the next exit buying another, and he knows that about himself as well as he knows anything.
Theo comes out of the store with two coffees, sees Jack already has one, and stops. He sees what’s in Jack’s other hand.
“Costigan —”
“I’m not opening it.”
Theo stands there in the sun with a coffee in each hand. “…Okay.” He looks past Jack at the van, at its open side door, and back, and whatever he sees there he keeps.

The van’s side door is open. Lena sits on its step with her jean jacket buttoned to the neck and her hands in its pockets, and she has seen all of it, from the counter through the glass to the air pump; he can see on her that she has. Her face is turned his way, and very still. The wind off the channel blows her hair across her face, and she lets it.

body.text: In his wallet, behind his father’s folded note, a strip of yellow legal pad says *Wed 2/17 · Lent*. He doesn’t take it out.

choices.text: *Put it in your breast pocket, where the tin used to ride.*
choices.key: At El Paso, under the same air pump, you bought a pack of Reds on the second day of Lent and didn’t open it. You put it in your breast pocket, where her tin used to ride.
response: He unbuttons the Carhartt’s breast pocket and slides the pack down beside the RAZR, into the worn place the tin made. It nearly fits. It’s a little too tall for the shape the tin left; he buttons the flap down over it anyway.

choices.key: At El Paso you bought a pack of Reds and didn’t open it. You held it out to Lena. You bought it, she said. You carry it.
response: He walks it over to the side door and holds it out to her, in the cold, at the length of his arm.
She looks at it. Her hands stay in her pockets.
“No,” Lena says. “You bought it. You carry it.”
He stands there with it held out a moment longer. Then the pack goes into the Carhartt’s breast pocket, in beside the phone, and he does up the button, and she watches him do the button.

choices.text: “It’s a hair shirt. With a Surgeon General’s warning.”
choices.key: At El Paso you bought a pack of Reds on the second day of Lent and didn’t open it. You told Theo it was a hair shirt with a Surgeon General’s warning.
response: “It’s a hair shirt,” Jack says. “With a Surgeon General’s warning.”

“That,” says Theo, “is the most Catholic thing I’ve ever seen.” He hands over the second coffee anyway, and Jack, a coffee in each hand now, gets the hair shirt into his breast pocket on the third try, wedged in behind the RAZR.

choices.text: *Don’t explain it to anybody. Get in the van.*
choices.key: At El Paso you bought a pack of Reds on the second day of Lent and didn’t open it. You didn’t explain it to anybody.
response: He doesn’t say a word to anybody. The pack goes into his breast pocket next to the phone, the button gets done, and he walks past Theo and his two coffees to the van.

s11a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:35 AM · EL PASO — THE SIDE WINDOW
body: The side door rolls shut on its track with Lena inside. Jack has the nozzle in pump four, the numbers turning over, and the store’s radio has gone on to somebody selling tires in Spanish.

body.text: Through the van’s side window she lifts one hand with all five fingers spread, and holds it up there, and puts it down, and looks at the road.
body.else: Through the glass she looks at the pack in his breast pocket for a long time, and then at the road.

body: The pump clicks off. Kevin, at the driver’s door, counts heads through the glass with one finger and gets seven, because Laney has the coconut up in the window. The pack rides where he put it, unopened, square against him under the canvas; once, as he hangs up the nozzle, his hand goes up to the flap and finds the button done, and comes away.

Out the back glass, past WHO DAT, the air pump gets small, and then the station, and then Juárez is a tan smear across the channel and gone behind an overpass. Out of El Paso the interstate bends north along the river, and a green sign comes up on the right: LAS CRUCES 44. Past it the Organ Mountains stand up out of the desert in a row of gray spires, the pipes of a church the size of New Mexico, which is the joke somebody already made when they named them. The pad is on his knee. Page three.
